extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, chymists, and learned readers interested in the foundations of chemical theory (17th-century experimental philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging theories about mixtion/mixture and the number/nature of elemental/principial substances, based on logical plausibility, experimental evidence, and careful interpretation of analyses. The page argues how to interpret chemical analyses, what counts as proof of elemental status, and warns against taking artisans' claims at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of mixtion (Aristotelian vs ancient/chymist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle (as interpreted) defines mistion as such a mutual penetration and perfect union that there is no portion of the mixed body, however minute, which does not contain all of the Four Elements; the ancients and many chymists hold instead that mixture is a juxta-position of separable corpuscles, each retaining its own nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the distinction to classify claims about mixtures: is the theory asserting perfect, indivisible union (Aristotelian) or an apposition/juxta-position where ingredients retain separable natures (ancients/chymists)? The text uses analogies (cloth woven of white and black threads, heaps of grain) to explain the latter notion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theories that yield absurd practical implications
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory about mixture should not imply manifestly ridiculous consequences (e.g., Aristotle's rule that a drop of wine added to ten thousand measures of water would be turned into water alone leads to absurd results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test theoretical definitions against common experience and practical operations (dilution, refining, metallurgy). If a hypothesis produces paradoxes when applied to simple cases (wine/water, alloying metals), this undermines its plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental recoverability as evidence of retained elemental nature
rubrics_metrics.description: If an ingredient of a compound can be recovered by chemical operations (e.g., aqua fortis dissolving silver while leaving gold as a black powder that can be reduced to gold), this indicates that the ingredient retained its nature in the mixture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to reproducible operations (distillation, dissolution, crystallization, cupellation/quartation) that separate components — those separations are evidence that components were not entirely destroyed but preserved in some form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral/functional indicators (predominant element governs motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable behaviors of a mixed body (e.g., motion tending toward the centre for earth-predominant bodies) indicate the active presence of predominant elements within the mixture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use macroscopic behaviors (motion, qualities) as empirical evidence about which principles are operative in a compound; such phenomena make the presence of elements plausible even if minute parts are not directly observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer an universal fixed number of elements without broad evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not proven that 'three' (or any specific number) is universally the number of distinct substances into which all mixed bodies resolve by fire; different compounds may yield different numbers of resolvable substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require comprehensive experimental support before declaring a universal number of principles; consider that some mixtures (glass, alloys) may require fewer or more elementary types and that analyses vary by subject and method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between artful skill and theoretical authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit skilled practitioners (artists/chymists) in their technical art, but do not accept their theoretical claims uncritically simply because they can produce effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat testimony of artisans as evidence of practical success, not as substitute for independent philosophical or experimental scrutiny of theoretical generalizations; do independent replication and conceptual analysis of what the art demonstrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require demonstration that alleged principles are uncompounded (true elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substances obtained by analysis and called 'principles' should not be assumed to be simple; one must examine whether they themselves are compounded rather than truly elementary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a chymical analysis produces distinct substances, investigate whether those substances are further analysable or composite before granting them status as primitive elements; reserve judgment until their (un)compounded nature is tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate matter immanent vs transient and common vs peculiar principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize distinctions: matter immanent (material parts that remain and retain nature in materiated things) vs transient (altered so as to receive new form), and common principles (e.g., Aristotelian four, chymists' tria prima) vs peculiar principles (specific to certain bodies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these classifications to refine arguments about what is preserved in mixtures and what counts as a principle; some purported principles may be accidental or peculiar and not universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret analytical results cautiously — permanence/indissolubility can indicate transmutation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a union produced (e.g., by mingling an 'elixir' with lead) is so indissoluble that no known operation separates the ingredients again, that permanence may indicate a transmutation (change of properties) rather than mere apposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider permanence and indissolubility as possible evidence for true change of substance (transmutation) rather than mere mixture; analyze whether the loss of former properties is accidental or substantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple kinds of argument: speculative plausibility and experimental evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments about the number and nature of elements should include both speculative considerations (reasoning about primary clusters, possible combinations) and empirical observations from experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance logical/conceptual models (e.g., coalitions of minute particles, possible variation in numbers of primary clusters) with reported and reproducible experimental outcomes; neither alone is decisive.
